prompt: The torque on an electric dipole in a uniform field is τ = pE sin θ. At what angle is the torque zero?

options.text: Zero degrees, with the dipole aligned along the field
Ninety degrees, with the dipole across the field
Forty-five degrees
The torque is never zero in a field
One hundred and eighty degrees only

explanation: sin 0 = 0, so the torque vanishes when the dipole lies along the field. That is the position the field twists it INTO: a dipole placed at an angle rotates until it is aligned, and then stops. The torque is greatest at 90 degrees, where sin is 1, because that is when the field has the most turning to do.

why.a: Correct. Aligned means sin θ = 0, so no torque.
why.b: Wrong. 90 degrees is where the torque is at its MAXIMUM.
why.c: Wrong. sin 45 is about 0.71, so the torque is substantial.
why.d: Wrong. It is zero at alignment, which is why dipoles line up.
why.e: Wrong. sin 180 is also zero, but so is sin 0, and 0 is the stable one.

prompt: The energy of a dipole in a field is U = minus pE cos θ, and it is at a minimum when the dipole is aligned with the field.
explanation: True. At θ = 0, cos 0 = 1, so U = minus pE, the most negative value available and therefore the minimum. Systems settle into their lowest energy, which is exactly why a dipole turns to align itself. The torque formula and the energy formula are telling the same story from two directions.

why.true: Correct. Aligned gives the most negative energy, which is the minimum.
why.false: Wrong. The minus sign in front makes cos θ = 1 the lowest energy, not the highest.

prompt: For a parallel plate capacitor, C = εᵣ ε₀ A over d, where A is the plate area and d is the {{1}} between the plates.
explanation: The separation, that is the gap. Closer plates mean a bigger capacitance, since d is in the denominator, which is why real capacitors use very thin insulating layers. Note that d is the gap, not the thickness of the metal.

topic: capacitors in parallel and in series
prompt: How do capacitors combine, compared with resistors?

options.text: Backwards: capacitors ADD in parallel, while resistors add in series
The same way as resistors in both cases
Capacitors add in series, and resistors add in parallel too
Capacitors always add, whichever way they are connected
Capacitors never simply add

explanation: Capacitors ADD in parallel: C = C1 + C2. In series they combine reciprocally, giving less than the smallest. Resistors are the exact opposite: they add in series and combine reciprocally in parallel. The hook is to learn ONE of them properly and flip it for the other. Physically, putting capacitors side by side is just making one bigger plate, so the capacitances add.

why.a: Correct, and remembering one and flipping is the reliable way to keep them apart.
why.b: Wrong. They behave oppositely, which is the whole difficulty.
why.d: Wrong. In series they combine reciprocally.
why.e: Wrong. In parallel they add straightforwardly.

prompt: Capacitors in series combine as 1 over C equivalent = 1 over C1 plus 1 over C2, which always gives a total LESS than the {{1}} capacitor in the combination.
explanation: Less than the smallest. That is a free check on every series answer: work it out, and if your total is not below the smallest capacitor you have forgotten to flip the reciprocal back. Test 1 question 2 uses it, where 1 and 5 microfarads in series give 0.833, below the 1.

prompt: Which of these is NOT an equivalent expression for the energy stored in a capacitor?

options.text: W = QV
W = one half CV squared
W = one half QV
W = Q squared over 2C
All four are equivalent

explanation: The three valid forms all carry a factor of one half: W = one half CV squared = one half QV = Q squared over 2C. QV without the half is wrong, and the half is there for a physical reason: the voltage climbed from zero to V as the capacitor charged, so the average voltage the charge crossed was V/2, not V. Forgetting it doubles the answer, and Test 1 question 15 offers exactly that wrong value.

why.a: Correct as the odd one out. QV has no half, so it is double the true energy.
why.b: Wrong choice: this IS a valid form, the one used most often.
why.c: Wrong choice: this is valid, and follows from C = Q/V.
why.d: Wrong choice: this is valid, and is the form to use when you know Q rather than V.
why.e: Wrong. QV is not among the valid forms.

prompt: Capacitance is the charge stored per volt applied, and its unit is the farad, which is one coulomb per {{1}}.
explanation: One coulomb per volt, straight from C = Q/V. The farad is a huge unit in practice, which is why real capacitors are quoted in microfarads, nanofarads and picofarads.

options.text: Two equal and opposite charges separated by a small distance
A single charge on a conductor
Two equal charges of the same sign
A conductor with no net charge
An insulator between capacitor plates

explanation: Two equal and opposite charges a small distance apart, with dipole moment p = qd pointing from the negative to the positive. The polarised atom is the everyday example: an applied field pulls the electron cloud one way and the nucleus the other, creating exactly this arrangement, which is what polarisation in an insulator means.

why.a: Correct. Two equal and opposite charges a small distance apart, with the dipole moment p = qd pointing from the negative charge to the positive one.
why.b: Wrong. A dipole needs two charges.
why.c: Wrong. They must be OPPOSITE, or the net effect cancels differently.
why.d: Wrong. A neutral conductor is not a dipole, though it can be polarised into one.
why.e: Wrong. That is a dielectric, though dielectrics work BY forming dipoles.

prompt: Match each quantity to what it describes.

pairs.right: How readily a material permits an ELECTRIC field
How readily a material permits a MAGNETIC field
Induced dipoles forming in an insulator under an applied field

explanation: The two names are deliberately parallel, and so are their roles: ε₀ appears in every electrostatic formula and μ₀ in every magnetic one. Their product is what gives the speed of light. Polarisation is the mechanism by which a dielectric raises capacitance.

prompt: Inserting a dielectric between capacitor plates always increases the capacitance.
explanation: True. C = εᵣ times C₀, and the relative permittivity εᵣ is always greater than 1 for a real material, being exactly 1 only for vacuum. The mechanism is polarisation: the dielectric's induced dipoles partly cancel the field between the plates, so the same charge sits at a lower voltage, and C = Q/V rises. Note it works the OPPOSITE way for the Coulomb force, which a dielectric divides by the same factor.

why.true: Correct. εᵣ is never less than 1, so C can only go up.
why.false: Wrong. You may be thinking of the Coulomb FORCE, which a dielectric reduces to F/K. Capacitance goes the other way.
